title: A metabolic–epigenetic pathway drives immune suppression in colorectal cancer
abstract: Tumor-associated neutrophils are being recognized as regulators of cancer immune evasion but the pathways that drive their pathogenic states remain unclear. A study now reveals a metabolic–chromatin crosstalk via a GSK3β–FH–fumarate–KDM2B axis that epigenetically reprograms neutrophils into an immunosuppressive state in colorectal cancer.

title: AI for detection of adverse events in the real world
abstract: Immune-related adverse events are common in cancer immunotherapy and can be difficult to recognize in clinical routine. Work now shows that an agentic AI system built around a large language model can identify such events in prospectively collected clinical notes and can make human review of such notes faster and more consistent.

title: A genome‑wide screen in E. coli reveals metabolic adaptations that enhance intratumoral fitness and bacterial cancer therapy efficacy
abstract: Despite decades of investigation, the fundamental molecular and cellular principles that enable bacteria to thrive within the tumor microenvironment have yet to be defined. Here, through a genome‑wide functional screen, we identify the bacterial genes and pathways that govern intratumoral fitness. Targeted deletion of nonglucose phosphotransferase systems to align bacterial metabolic preference with tumor metabolite availability promotes bacterial intratumoral fitness. Integrating multiple metabolic adaptations into a single tumor‑avid Escherichia coli strain (Ec‑TA) results in increased tumor colonization, not only after intratumoral delivery but also after intravenous delivery, leading to increased anti‑tumor efficacy when using Ec‑TA engineered to deliver an encoded immunostimulatory payload. Furthermore, Ec‑TA displaces wild‑type bacteria from pre‑colonized tumors when administered systemically, underscoring its potential for locally delivering therapeutics in the presence of resident tumor microbes. These data demonstrate that adapting bacteria to the unique characteristics of the tumor metabolic microenvironment can drive the development of safer and more effective chassis for next‑generation bacterial cancer therapies.

title: An agentic AI system enhances clinical detection of immune-related adverse events in a multi-phase validation study
abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) affect up to 40% of patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet identification requires laborious, inconsistent manual chart review. Here we show that agentic artificial intelligence coupled with human verification could enhance efficiency, performance and consistency for irAE assessment. We developed and evaluated an agentic large language model system to extract the presence, temporality, severity grade, attribution and certainty of six irAE types from clinical notes. Retrospectively, the system achieved a macro-averaged F 1 of 0.92 for current-event detection and 0.66 for multi-class severity grading; self-consistency improved F 1 by 0.14. The best-performing configuration cost approximately US$0.02 per note. In prospective silent deployment over 3 months, the binary F 1 was 0.72–0.79. In a randomized crossover study of clinical trial staff, agentic assistance reduced annotation time by 2.71 min ( P < 0.001), increased complete-match accuracy (odds ratio 1.45; 95% confidence interval 1.01–2.08; P = 0.045) and improved interannotator agreement (Krippendorff’s α from 0.22–0.51 to 0.82–0.85).

title: GALE is a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint of Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing
abstract: Vγ9Vδ2 T cells mediate HLA-independent targeting of tumor cells, offering unique opportunities for cancer immunotherapy, yet their therapeutic efficacy remains limited. Here, using a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify UDP-galactose 4-epimerase (GALE) as a tumor-intrinsic checkpoint that restricts Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated killing. GALE is a key nucleotide-sugar metabolic enzyme that controls the interconversion of UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose, thereby supporting protein glycosylation and cell-surface glycan remodeling. Mechanistically, GALE promotes complex N-glycosylation of CD155 and CEACAM1, favoring their engagement with the inhibitory receptors TIGIT and TIM3, respectively, while limiting CD155 binding to the activating receptor CD226. GALE loss potentiates Vγ9Vδ2 T cell-mediated tumor killing in multiple mouse models and colorectal cancer patient-derived organoids. Together, these findings reveal how nucleotide-sugar metabolism shapes tumor–immune communication through complex N-glycan remodeling and identify GALE and its downstream receptor–ligand interactions as potential therapeutic targets for enhancing Vγ9Vδ2 T cell antitumor activity.

title: BAZ2A-induced epigenetic states in cancer cells fuel palmitate accumulation in the tumor microenvironment driving CAR-T cell exhaustion
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy shows limited efficacy in solid tumors, partly owing to poorly defined tumor-intrinsic resistance mechanisms. Here we show that the epigenetic regulator BAZ2A drives resistance to CD70-targeted CAR-T therapy by reprogramming tumor lipid metabolism. Using an in vivo CRISPR screen in a mouse renal cell carcinoma model, we identify BAZ2A as a key mediator that promotes the production and accumulation of palmitic acid, a saturated fatty acid in the tumor microenvironment. Excess palmitic acid is taken up by CAR-T cells and impairs mitochondrial fitness by inhibiting PGC-1α activity, thereby enforcing a dysfunctional state. Pharmacologic inhibition of BAZ2A reduces lipid accumulation and restores CAR-T cell activity in vivo. These findings reveal an epigenetic–metabolic mechanism of immune resistance and suggest that targeting tumor lipid remodeling represents a therapeutic strategy to overcome CAR-T resistance in solid tumors.

title: ANO6-mediated trogocytosis of cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes pancreatic cancer cell growth and immune suppression
abstract: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the fibroblastic stroma constitutes most of the tumor mass and is remarkably devoid of functional blood vessels, leaving unresolved how PDAC cells obtain essential metabolites and water-insoluble lipids. We find that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) acquire and transfer lipids from blood-borne particles to PDAC cells through trogocytosis of CAF plasma membranes, a process requiring the CAF-expressed phospholipid scramblase anoctamin 6 (ANO6) to promote PDAC cell survival. Cancer cells and CAFs form synapse-like contacts that induce cytosolic calcium influx in CAFs through Orai channels, activating ANO6 and driving phosphatidylserine exposure on CAF membranes, which initiates trogocytosis and transfer of membrane lipids, including cholesterol, to PDAC cells. This ANO6-dependent phosphatidylserine externalization also supports CAF-mediated immunosuppression of cytotoxic T cells through trogocytosis. Blockade of ANO6 antagonizes tumor growth, partly by disrupting cholesterol delivery to cancer cells, and attenuates immune suppression, identifying ANO6 as a candidate therapeutic target in PDAC.

title: Targeting GALE harnesses γδ T cells for cancer immunotherapy
abstract: Cancer cells can evade the immune system through mechanisms such as downregulation of MHC I molecules and expression of inhibitory ligands. Research now shows that targeting the metabolic enzyme GALE in tumor cells boosts the killing of these cells by γδ T cells through altering the glycosylation of key immune-checkpoint ligands.

title: Myeloid-derived TGFβ1 and oncostatin M establish two distinct stromal niches controlling late and hybrid EMT states
abstract: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) regulates tumor progression, metastasis and resistance to therapy. EMT encompasses a continuum of tumor states displaying different functions. The precise dialog between the tumor microenvironment and the different EMT states remains poorly understood. Using single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of mouse skin tumors, we uncover that different EMT states are associated with different niches. Neutrophils are more abundant in niches associated with hybrid EMT and secreted oncostatin M, which partially activates EMT while sustaining the epithelial program, promoting hybrid EMT states and metastasis formation. Macrophages are more abundant in niches associated with more advanced EMT states, which, together with other stromal cells, express TGFβ1 that promotes the late EMT state. Oncostatin M and TGFβ1 function in a feed-forward manner by creating distinct inflammatory niches to maintain specific EMT states. Together, our results reveal that distinct niches are associated with specific EMT states and that signaling pathways sustain their own niche’s identity by recruiting specific myeloid cell populations.

title: Oncostatin M and TGFβ1 divide the epithelial–mesenchymal landscape
abstract: Stabilization of the hybrid epithelial–mesenchymal state drives therapy resistance and metastasic progression. Dong et al. use integrated single-cell and spatial analyses to demonstrate that oncostatin M and TGFβ1, respectively, maintain hybrid and late epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition states within self-sustaining neutrophil- and macrophage-rich niches of squamous cell carcinoma.

title: Basophils inhibit early lung metastasis by suppressing regulatory T cells
abstract: Basophils are rare cells best known for their role in allergy but their contribution to cancer remains poorly understood. Here, we found that basophils suppress early lung metastatic seeding in mice by enhancing antitumor CD8 + T cell immunity through inhibition of regulatory T (T reg ) cells. Basophils restrain T reg cells through two complementary mechanisms: mast cell protease 8-mediated cleavage of interleukin-2 receptor α and histamine-mediated activation of the histamine H1 receptor (HRH1). HRH1 blockade with loratadine abolished T reg cell suppression and accelerated metastatic seeding in mice. In a prospective double-blind crossover trial of loratadine versus placebo enrolling 40 healthy volunteers ( IRCT20170608034390N14 ), circulating T reg cell frequency (primary outcome) increased following loratadine. Higher blood basophil counts predicted improved survival across human cancers and integrative multiomic analyses identified conserved quiescent (B0) and tumor-associated (B1) basophil states, with B0 predicting favorable outcomes. These findings identify basophils as regulators of early metastatic progression and highlight the basophil–T reg cell axis as a potential therapeutic target.
